subjective.topic: Ideology of Pakistan and Two-Nation Theory
subjective.question: Define ideology and explain the importance of the Ideology of Pakistan.
subjective.answer: An ideology is a system of ideas, beliefs and values that explains the world and guides the conduct of a nation. The Ideology of Pakistan is the set of beliefs, based on Islam and the Two-Nation Theory, which held that the Muslims of the Subcontinent were a separate nation entitled to a homeland of their own. Its importance is great: (1) it provided the very basis for the demand and creation of Pakistan; (2) it unites the people of Pakistan's different regions and languages into one nation; (3) it sets the goal of an Islamic welfare state where laws conform to the Quran and Sunnah; (4) it gives direction to the constitution and national policies; and (5) it preserves the separate cultural identity of the Muslims of the Subcontinent.

subjective.topic: Ideology of Pakistan and Two-Nation Theory
subjective.question: What is unique about the ideology of Pakistan?
subjective.answer: The uniqueness of Pakistan's ideology is that Pakistan is the only state in the world created purely on the basis of an ideology - Islam - rather than on race, language, colour or territory. The people of its regions spoke different languages and belonged to different ethnic groups, yet they united under the single bond of Islam and the Two-Nation Theory. Its ideology is derived from the eternal principles of the Quran and Sunnah, so it does not change with time, and it aims at establishing an Islamic welfare state ensuring justice, equality and protection of minorities.

subjective.topic: Ideology of Pakistan and Two-Nation Theory
subjective.question: Explain the Two-Nation Theory and its main bases.
subjective.answer: The Two-Nation Theory states that the Muslims and Hindus of the Subcontinent were two separate nations with different religions, cultures, laws, customs, heroes and ways of life, and therefore could not live together permanently in one state. Its main bases are: (1) Religion - Islam is a complete code of life, entirely different from Hinduism; (2) Culture and society - different festivals, food, dress and social customs; (3) Law - Muslims follow Islamic law of inheritance and marriage, Hindus follow their own; (4) Heroes and history - the heroes of one nation are the villains of the other; and (5) Language and literature - Urdu versus Hindi. Events like the Urdu-Hindi Controversy (1867) and the Congress ministries (1937-39) proved the theory in practice.

subjective.topic: Sir Syed Ahmed Khan and the Aligarh Movement
subjective.question: Describe the traditional education system of the Muslims before 1857.
subjective.answer: Before 1857, Muslim education in the Subcontinent was traditional and religious in character. It was imparted in maktabs and madrassas attached to mosques, where the Quran, Hadith, Fiqh, Arabic, Persian, logic and Islamic philosophy were taught. Education was free and financed by endowments (waqf) and wealthy patrons. Persian was the language of instruction and administration, while modern sciences, English and technical subjects were almost entirely absent. After 1857 this system decayed because Muslim endowments were confiscated and Persian was replaced by English in offices, leaving Muslims educationally and economically backward - the gap Sir Syed Ahmed Khan later tried to fill through modern education.

subjective.topic: Sir Syed Ahmed Khan and the Aligarh Movement
subjective.question: What were the movements and efforts of Sir Syed Ahmed Khan for the promotion of modern education among the Muslims?
subjective.answer: After the War of 1857, Sir Syed Ahmed Khan concluded that Muslim progress was impossible without modern Western education. His efforts include: (1) he established schools at Muradabad (1859) and Ghazipur (1862); (2) he founded the Scientific Society (1864) to translate English books on science and literature into Urdu; (3) he started the journal Tahzib-ul-Akhlaq (1870) to reform Muslim society and create a taste for learning; (4) he founded the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental (MAO) School at Aligarh in 1875, raised to a college in 1877, which combined Western sciences with Islamic teachings; and (5) he organised the Muhammadan Educational Conference (1886) to spread the message of education all over India. These efforts produced a new generation of educated Muslim leaders.

subjective.topic: Sir Syed Ahmed Khan and the Aligarh Movement
subjective.question: Describe the role and aims of the Aligarh Movement.
subjective.answer: The Aligarh Movement was the educational, social and political reform movement led by Sir Syed Ahmed Khan centred at the MAO College, Aligarh. Its aims were: (1) to promote modern Western education among the Muslims while retaining Islamic values; (2) to remove misunderstandings between the Muslims and the British and win British goodwill after 1857; (3) to reform Muslim society by ending outdated customs through Tahzib-ul-Akhlaq; (4) to prepare Muslims for government service and economic competition with Hindus; and (5) to keep Muslims away from the Congress, which Sir Syed considered a Hindu-dominated body. Its role was historic: it revived Muslim confidence, produced the leadership that later ran the Pakistan Movement, and its college became the 'arsenal of Muslim India'.

subjective.topic: Muslim League, Iqbal and Quaid-e-Azam
subjective.question: Why did the Muslims establish a separate political platform, the All-India Muslim League, in 1906?
subjective.answer: The Muslims established the All-India Muslim League at Dhaka on 30 December 1906 for several reasons: (1) the Indian National Congress, founded in 1885, had proved to be a Hindu-dominated body that ignored Muslim interests; (2) the Urdu-Hindi Controversy (1867) and Hindu revivalist movements showed that Hindus would not protect Muslim rights; (3) the partition of Bengal (1905), favourable to Muslims, was opposed bitterly by Hindus, alarming Muslim leaders; (4) the Simla Deputation (October 1906) had won the Viceroy's promise of separate electorates, and a permanent political organisation was needed to safeguard such gains; and (5) Muslims needed their own platform to present their demands before the government and to protect their political, religious and cultural rights.

subjective.topic: Muslim League, Iqbal and Quaid-e-Azam
subjective.question: Why did Allama Iqbal turn from Western themes to writing poetry for the Muslims of the Subcontinent?
subjective.answer: In his early poetry Iqbal wrote on universal and Western themes, but his stay in Europe (1905-1908) changed him. He observed Western materialism, nationalism and moral decline closely and became disillusioned with them. At the same time he saw the miserable condition of the Muslims of India - politically weak, educationally backward and losing faith in themselves. Iqbal therefore turned his poetry into an instrument of Muslim revival: through works like Shikwa, Jawab-e-Shikwa, Bang-e-Dara and his Persian poetry he preached selfhood (Khudi), faith and unity, awakened the Muslims from slumber, and prepared them mentally for a separate homeland, which he finally demanded in his Allahabad Address of 1930.

subjective.topic: Muslim League, Iqbal and Quaid-e-Azam
subjective.question: Discuss Allama Iqbal's critiques of Indian nationalism.
subjective.answer: Allama Iqbal strongly criticised the Indian (territorial) nationalism preached by the Congress on several grounds: (1) he held that nationalism based on territory was a Western idea that divided humanity and caused wars in Europe; (2) Islam, he argued, is a universal brotherhood and cannot be confined within geographical boundaries, so for Muslims religion, not land, is the basis of nationhood; (3) in India, 'one nation' in practice meant the permanent rule of the Hindu majority, which would swallow Muslim culture and identity; (4) he believed the Congress demand of a united India was a device to establish Hindu domination; and (5) he therefore concluded that the Muslims of the North-West were a nation by themselves and should have a separate state where they could live according to Islam, as demanded in the Allahabad Address (1930).

subjective.topic: Muslim League, Iqbal and Quaid-e-Azam
subjective.question: Write down the main points of Quaid-e-Azam's Fourteen Points (1929).
subjective.answer: Quaid-e-Azam presented the Fourteen Points in 1929 in response to the Nehru Report. Their main points were: (1) India should have a federal constitution with residuary powers vested in the provinces; (2) all provinces should enjoy uniform provincial autonomy; (3) minorities should have adequate representation in all legislatures and elected bodies; (4) Muslims should have one-third representation in the Central Legislature; (5) separate electorates for Muslims should be retained; (6) no territorial redistribution should affect the Muslim majority in Punjab, Bengal and NWFP; (7) full religious liberty should be guaranteed to all communities; (8) no bill should be passed if three-fourths of a community's members opposed it; (9) Sindh should be separated from Bombay; (10) reforms should be introduced in NWFP and Balochistan; and (11) Muslims should have an adequate share in the services and in cabinets at the centre and in the provinces.

subjective.topic: Government of India Act 1935 and Congress Rule
subjective.question: What were the reasons behind the enactment of the Government of India Act 1935?
subjective.answer: The Government of India Act 1935 was enacted because: (1) the Government of India Act 1919 and dyarchy had failed to satisfy Indian political opinion; (2) the Simon Commission (1927) had reviewed the constitutional problem and recommended provincial autonomy and a federation; (3) the three Round Table Conferences (1930-32) in London discussed a new constitutional framework; (4) the growing freedom movement, including the Civil Disobedience Movement, forced the British to offer further reforms; and (5) the British wanted an All-India Federation including the princely states, which would safeguard British interests while granting limited self-government in the provinces. The Act therefore introduced provincial autonomy and proposed a federation at the centre.

subjective.topic: Government of India Act 1935 and Congress Rule
subjective.question: Explain the three Legislative Lists introduced under the Government of India Act 1935.
subjective.answer: The Government of India Act 1935 divided legislative powers between the centre and the provinces through three lists: (1) The Federal (Central) List contained subjects of all-India importance such as defence, foreign affairs, railways, currency and posts, on which only the Federal Legislature could make laws; (2) The Provincial List contained subjects of local importance such as education, health, agriculture, police and local government, reserved for the Provincial Legislatures; and (3) The Concurrent List contained subjects such as criminal law, civil procedure, marriage and factories, on which both the Federal and Provincial Legislatures could legislate, though in case of a conflict the federal law prevailed. Residuary powers were left to the discretion of the Governor-General.

subjective.topic: Government of India Act 1935 and Congress Rule
subjective.question: Describe the provincial part (provincial autonomy) of the Government of India Act 1935.
subjective.answer: Under the provincial part of the Government of India Act 1935, dyarchy was abolished in the provinces and provincial autonomy was introduced. All provincial subjects were transferred to ministers responsible to the elected provincial legislatures, so for the first time responsible government operated in the provinces. The Governor remained the head of the province with special powers to safeguard minorities and British interests, and he could take over the administration in an emergency. The franchise was extended to about one-sixth of the population. Provincial autonomy actually came into operation after the elections of 1937, when popular ministries, mostly of the Congress, took office in the provinces.

subjective.topic: Government of India Act 1935 and Congress Rule
subjective.question: What was the impact of the Congress success in the elections of 1937 on the Muslims?
subjective.answer: In the elections of 1937 the Congress won majorities and formed ministries in eight provinces. Its rule (1937-39) had a deep impact on the Muslims: (1) the Congress refused to share power with the Muslim League and demanded that League members merge into the Congress; (2) Hindu cultural policies were imposed - Bande Mataram was made compulsory, the Wardha Scheme of education and Hindi were promoted, and Urdu was discouraged; (3) Muslims suffered discrimination in services and local bodies, and anti-Muslim riots went unchecked, as documented in the Pirpur Report (1938) and the Sharif Report; and (4) these experiences convinced the Muslims that in a united India they would live under permanent Hindu domination. As a result the Muslim League became a mass movement, the Two-Nation Theory gained universal acceptance among Muslims, and when the Congress ministries resigned in 1939 the League celebrated the Day of Deliverance.

subjective.topic: Final Phase of the Pakistan Movement
subjective.question: What was the objective of the Lahore Resolution of 1940?
subjective.answer: The objective of the Lahore Resolution, passed by the Muslim League on 23 March 1940, was to declare that no constitutional plan would be acceptable to the Muslims unless the Muslim-majority regions of the North-West and the East were grouped to constitute independent, autonomous and sovereign states. In simple words, its objective was to secure a separate homeland (or homelands) for the Muslims of the Subcontinent where they could live according to their religion and culture, free from Hindu domination. It rejected the idea of a single federal centre for a united India and thus set the clear final goal - Pakistan - before the Pakistan Movement.

subjective.topic: Final Phase of the Pakistan Movement
subjective.question: How did the failure of the Cabinet Mission Plan contribute to the demand for the partition of India?
subjective.answer: The Cabinet Mission Plan (1946) was the last attempt to preserve a united India through a three-tier federation with grouping of provinces. The Muslim League accepted it because the compulsory grouping of Muslim-majority provinces (Groups B and C) contained the seed of Pakistan. However, Congress accepted it with its own interpretation, and Nehru's statement of 10 July 1946 that the Constituent Assembly would not be bound by the Plan destroyed its basis. The League withdrew its acceptance and resorted to Direct Action. The collapse of the Plan proved that Congress would not honour any arrangement protecting Muslim interests within a united India, convinced even moderate opinion that coexistence was impossible, and made partition the only remaining solution, finally accepted in the 3 June 1947 Plan.

subjective.topic: Final Phase of the Pakistan Movement
subjective.question: What was Direct Action Day (16 August 1946)? Explain its causes and consequences.
subjective.answer: Direct Action Day was observed by the Muslim League on 16 August 1946 to press its demand for Pakistan. Its causes were: (1) the failure of the Cabinet Mission Plan after Congress's reservations and Nehru's statement that the Constituent Assembly was sovereign and unbound; (2) the Viceroy's decision to invite only the Congress to form the interim government, ignoring the League; and (3) the League's decision to withdraw its acceptance of the Plan and use 'direct action' to achieve Pakistan. Its consequences were severe: Calcutta witnessed terrible communal riots (the Great Calcutta Killing) in which thousands were killed, and violence spread to Noakhali and Bihar. The tragedy hardened communal divisions, demonstrated that Hindus and Muslims could no longer live under one government, and hastened the British decision to partition India in 1947.

subjective.topic: Final Phase of the Pakistan Movement
subjective.question: Discuss the role of students in the creation of Pakistan.
subjective.answer: Students played a heroic role in the Pakistan Movement. The All-India Muslim Students Federation, founded in 1937, organised Muslim students on one platform. The students of Aligarh Muslim University - which Quaid-e-Azam called the 'arsenal of Muslim India' - carried the League's message to every corner of the country. During the crucial elections of 1945-46, students went from door to door, worked as volunteers, and persuaded voters to support the League, contributing to its sweeping victory in the Muslim seats. Students also spread political awareness through speeches, pamphlets and processions, raised funds, and faced arrests and police action. Quaid-e-Azam repeatedly praised them, saying that the students had rendered the greatest service to the cause of Pakistan.

subjective.topic: Constitutional Development of Pakistan
subjective.question: Write a short note on the Objectives Resolution.
subjective.answer: The Objectives Resolution was passed by the Constituent Assembly of Pakistan on 12 March 1949 and was moved by the first Prime Minister, Liaquat Ali Khan. It declared that sovereignty over the entire universe belongs to Allah Almighty and that the authority exercised by the people of Pakistan is a sacred trust within the limits prescribed by Him. It promised that Muslims would be enabled to order their lives according to the Quran and Sunnah, that minorities would be fully protected, that fundamental rights would be guaranteed, and that Pakistan would be a federal, democratic state. It has served as the preamble of the constitutions of 1956, 1962 and 1973, and in 1985 it was made a substantive part of the Constitution as Article 2-A.

subjective.topic: Constitutional Development of Pakistan
subjective.question: Discuss the importance of the Objectives Resolution in the constitutional development of Pakistan.
subjective.answer: The Objectives Resolution is the most important document in Pakistan's constitutional history. Its importance is that: (1) it was the first constitutional document adopted by Pakistan's own Constituent Assembly and fixed the Islamic and democratic character of the future state; (2) it laid down the guiding principles - sovereignty of Allah, democracy, fundamental rights, federalism, independence of judiciary and protection of minorities - on which all later constitutions were framed; (3) it was retained as the preamble of the constitutions of 1956, 1962 and 1973, giving continuity to the constitutional process despite repeated breakdowns; (4) it balanced Islamic principles with modern democratic values, assuring minorities of their rights; and (5) in 1985 it became a substantive, enforceable part of the Constitution as Article 2-A, so it now guides the legislature and the courts in interpreting the Constitution.

subjective.topic: Constitutional Development of Pakistan
subjective.question: State three functions of the Council of Common Interests (CCI).
subjective.answer: The Council of Common Interests, established under Article 153 of the Constitution of 1973 and chaired by the Prime Minister, performs the following functions: (1) it formulates and regulates policies in relation to matters in Part II of the Federal Legislative List, such as railways, mineral oil and natural gas, electricity and major ports, and supervises and controls the related institutions; (2) it decides disputes between the federation and the provinces, or between provinces, relating to the sharing of river waters and other Part II subjects; and (3) it serves as a forum of coordination between the federal and provincial governments, promoting harmony and uniform policy on subjects of common interest.

subjective.topic: Constitutional Development of Pakistan
subjective.question: Give reasons for the failure of the Constitution of 1956.
subjective.answer: The first Constitution of Pakistan (1956) failed and was abrogated in October 1958 for several reasons: (1) political instability - governments changed frequently, with seven prime ministers between 1951 and 1958, and no party commanded stable support; (2) weak and divided political parties lacked discipline and ideology and indulged in floor-crossing; (3) the controversial One Unit scheme and the parity formula created resentment in East Pakistan and smaller provinces; (4) provincialism and the language issue (Bengali versus Urdu) weakened national unity; (5) general elections under the new constitution were repeatedly postponed, so it never gained democratic legitimacy; (6) the bureaucracy and the army had become powerful under Governor-General Ghulam Muhammad's era and interfered in politics; and (7) President Iskander Mirza's own ambitions led him to abrogate the constitution and impose martial law with General Ayub Khan.

subjective.topic: Constitutional Development of Pakistan
subjective.question: Write down the salient features of the Constitution of 1973.
subjective.answer: The main features of the Constitution of 1973 are: (1) it is a written and comparatively rigid constitution, enforced on 14 August 1973; (2) it establishes a federal system with four provinces and a bicameral parliament - the National Assembly and the Senate; (3) it provides a parliamentary form of government in which the Prime Minister is the chief executive; (4) Islam is declared the state religion and no law can be made repugnant to the Quran and Sunnah; (5) it guarantees comprehensive fundamental rights to all citizens; (6) it provides an independent judiciary with a Supreme Court and High Courts; (7) Urdu is the national language; and (8) it created institutions like the Council of Common Interests and the National Finance Commission to manage federation-province relations.

subjective.topic: Background: Decline of the Mughal Empire
subjective.question: How did Aurangzeb's policies contribute to the decline of the Mughal Empire?
subjective.answer: Aurangzeb's policies contributed greatly to the decline of the Mughal Empire: (1) his religious orthodoxy and intolerance - reimposing the Jizya (1679), destroying temples and executing the Sikh Guru Tegh Bahadur - alienated Hindus, Sikhs and Rajputs whose support had been the empire's strength under Akbar; (2) his endless wars in the Deccan against the Marathas and the southern states kept him away from the north for 25 years, emptied the treasury and ruined administration; (3) his annexations over-extended the empire beyond what could be governed with the communications of the age; (4) his suspicion of his sons and nobles weakened the mansabdari system and central control; and (5) the Maratha, Sikh, Jat and Rajput revolts he provoked continued after his death in 1707, breaking the empire into pieces under his weak successors.
